name: Nefiracetam
lead: Nefiracetam (code DM-9384) is an oral racetam-class nootropic developed in Japan and studied for dementia, post-stroke depression and post-stroke apathy.[1][13] It is unscheduled in the United States and prescription-only (Schedule 4) in Australia.[1]

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums, racetams are discussed as focus and motivation aids, and nefiracetam appears occasionally on lists of lesser-known options.[14] The appearance connection claimed by users is indirect: better drive and concentration are said to help people keep up training, skincare and grooming routines. No study has measured appearance outcomes with nefiracetam.
Research on the compound consists of laboratory pharmacology, animal memory models, and a small set of human trials in stroke patients and Alzheimer's disease.[2][3][5][6][7][8]
infobox: Investigational; Schedule 4 in Australia, unscheduled in the US[1]

paras: No approved or studied appearance use exists. A long-running strength-training forum thread on cognitive boosters mentions nefiracetam only as an obscure racetam.[14] Reported motivations for racetams in general are focus, mood and drive rather than any direct effect on skin, hair or body.

Nefiracetam has been investigated for cerebrovascular and Alzheimer's-type dementia and for apathy and depression after stroke.[1][13] Apathy occurs in roughly 20-25% of people after stroke, according to a review, which has made it a target for motivation-enhancing drugs.[10]

Nefiracetam is chemically N-(2,6-dimethylphenyl)-2-(2-oxopyrrolidin-1-yl)acetamide, with the formula C14H18N2O2 and a molar mass of about 246 g/mol; it is classed as an acetanilide and shares the pyrrolidone ring of the racetam family [1].

The compound carries the development code DM-9384 and was profiled in Current Opinion in Investigational Drugs under the name of the Japanese company Daiichi Seiyaku [15]. Early phase I and early phase II studies were reported from Japan in 1994 [1], and a later drug profile lists the codes DM 9384 and DZL 221 and the name Translon [13]. Later work shifted to post-stroke apathy and depression, with registered trials running from 1999 (Alzheimer's) to 2014 (stroke apathy) [6][7][8].

Laboratory studies reported enhancement of neuronal calcium channel currents,[2] modulation of acetylcholine receptor currents through two signalling pathways,[3] and increased turnover of GABAergic components in rat cortex.[4] Later work found potentiation of NMDA-evoked currents in rat cortical neurons, with a bell-shaped dose-response curve, and implicated CaM kinase II and related signalling.[12]

Wikipedia also describes high affinity for the GABA-A receptor, where it is presumed to act as an agonist, unlike other racetams, and notes that no commonly accepted unified mechanism has been established for the piracetam-like nootropics as a class.[1][11]

Wikipedia reports an IC50 of 8.5 nM at the GABA-A receptor, with about 80% of muscimol binding displaced, and notes that in mice it reversed amnesia induced by picrotoxin and bicuculline without preventing the seizures those drugs cause [1].
It is taken orally and has an elimination half-life of roughly 3-5 hours in healthy volunteers.[1]
A phase 2 trial in Alzheimer's disease (n=50) was registered in 1999.[6] Early phase I and II studies under the code DM-9384 were reported in Japan in the 1990s.[1][13]

A randomised, double-blind trial of 159 people with major depression within three months of stroke compared nefiracetam with placebo and did not find a significant time-by-treatment interaction on depression scores; response rates exceeded 70% and remission rates 40% in both arms, with a possible signal in the most severely depressed subgroup.[8] A companion analysis examined apathy within the same population.[9]
A two-centre randomised, placebo-controlled trial in Perth, Western Australia, ran from 2010 to 2014 in patients with recent stroke and apathy.[7] No trial has examined appearance outcomes.

Wikipedia summarises the preliminary human work as suggesting possible improvement of apathy and motivation after stroke and antiamnesic effects in Alzheimer's-type and cerebrovascular dementia, and adds that long-term human and primate studies showed no toxicity [1]. The Perth trial enrolled patients hospitalised with stroke who were diagnosed with apathy 8 to 36 days after the event [7].

In animals, renal and testicular toxicity was seen, particularly in dogs, attributed to a metabolite (M-18) that humans and primates do not form; rats required higher doses and monkeys showed none.[1] The same source states that no toxicity was reported in clinical trials.[1] A forum post in a long-running nootropics thread repeats the testicular-toxicity point as hearsay.[14]

Nefiracetam is not approved as a medicine in the United States or most other markets and is unscheduled in the US, while Australia lists it as prescription-only.[1] It circulates in nootropic and bodybuilding communities as one of many racetams, alongside piracetam, aniracetam and pramiracetam.[14] Reviews of the racetam family describe a long history of cognitive-enhancer claims alongside limited clinical confirmation.[11]

timeline.event: Rat studies describe DM-9384 effects on GABAergic turnover.[4]
Calcium channel enhancement reported; phase I and early phase II studies published in Japan.[1][2]

lore.intro: Nefiracetam is mentioned only occasionally in strength and nootropic forums, typically within wider racetam discussions.[14]

claims.claim: Racetams such as nefiracetam are a way to boost focus and brain function.
claims.believers: Forum users list racetams among options for cognitive boosting and mention nefiracetam as a rarer one.[14]
claims.experts: Published human trials of nefiracetam involve stroke and dementia populations and did not test focus or appearance in healthy users.[7][8]

claims.believers: Forum posters mention the toxicity as a reason it is harder to recommend.[14]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports toxicity in dogs from a metabolite humans do not form and none in clinical trials.[1]

card.summary: A Japanese racetam studied for dementia and post-stroke apathy, with no appearance evidence.

quick.overview:
Nefiracetam is a racetam studied for dementia and apathy after stroke. It is sold online as a nootropic.

No source links it to appearance.
quick.mechanism: Lab studies point to effects on calcium channels, acetylcholine receptors and the GABA system.
quick.risks: Animal toxicity (kidney, testis) was seen in dogs; human trials reported none. Prescription-only in Australia.

chain: Users report focus or drive effects
Routines (training, grooming, study) are kept up more consistently
angle.text: Forum users who take racetams describe them as a way to sharpen focus and motivation, which they link to sticking with training and self-care routines. This is a user-reported chain; published work on nefiracetam concerns cognition and post-stroke apathy rather than looks.
